items.q: What is SCADask?
items.a: SCADask is the applied research studio at the Savannah College of Art and Design. It works with students, faculty, and industry on original research, published reports, and emerging technology experiments. Its research examines creativity, commerce, culture, and technology.

items.q: What does AI Insights 2026 find?
alt: What’s the takeaway from AI Insights 2026?
What did the 2026 AI research reveal?
items.a: AI Insights 2026 identifies research synthesis and content generation as the highest-impact areas for AI adoption. As AI handles more production tasks, creative value shifts toward human judgment and direction, with creative direction identified as the human skill growing most in value. The full findings, survey data, and contributor perspectives are in the report PDF.

items.q: How was SplatGarden made?
alt: How did student work become an interactive garden?
items.a: SplatGarden combines procedural plant growth, simulation, and AI-stylized textures using tools including Houdini and Unreal Engine. The team captured 990 images of the garden and trained them into roughly 3 million Gaussian splats for real-time playback. A browser-based experience built with Spark and Three.js adds gesture controls, interactive effects, and painterly styling.

items.q: What is SplatGarden, and when was the case study published?
alt: What does the Spring 2026 case study cover?
items.a: SplatGarden turns student work into an interactive, real-time 3D garden where visitors can explore the scene and discover how its assets were made. The case study is labeled Spring 2026.

items.q: How can visitors interact with SplatGarden?
alt: What can I do in the garden?
Can I control it with my hands?
Can I open the live garden?
items.a: The page offers an “Open the live garden” option to explore the interactive scene. In-browser hand tracking lets a single-hand pinch orbit the scene, a quick pinch-tap trigger a click effect, and a two-hand spread or contract adjust zoom. Clicks and gestures also trigger effects in the garden.

items.q: How does SplatGarden use Gaussian splatting?
alt: How was the garden turned into 3D?
How many Gaussians are in the scene?
items.a: Gaussian splatting transforms photographs into a 3D scene that can be viewed from different perspectives in real time. For SplatGarden, the team rendered 990 images from different angles inside the original Unreal Engine environment. Training those images in PostShot produced approximately 3 million Gaussians optimized for real-time playback.

items.q: How were the garden's flowers and growing vines created?
alt: How was the grape hyacinth built?
What plant tools did the team use?
items.a: Two custom Houdini tools recreated grape hyacinth and daffodil growth, using golden-angle floret placement for hyacinths and KineFX rigging with Vellum simulation for daffodil petal motion. In Unreal Engine, a real-time GPU workflow controls vine stem growth and deformation. The Motion Design plugin adds flowers and leaves, with Sequencer and Blueprint driving the blooming sequence.

items.q: How were AI tools used to create the garden's painterly look?
alt: How did they make painterly textures?
What does the AI stylization tool do?
How was the style reference used?
items.a: A custom AI stylization tool combined shapes and structure from realistic textures with the look of a chosen style reference. This produced painterly textures while preserving underlying detail. The results were then refined in Houdini's COP Network and Substance Painter.

items.q: How was foliage built and placed throughout the garden?
alt: How did they place the plants?
Why use both PCG and foliage painting?
What tools made the environment assets?
items.a: The team procedurally modeled foliage in SpeedTree, optimizing polygon counts for real-time performance, then created painterly textures in Substance Designer. Procedural Content Generation handled large-scale distribution across the environment. Unreal Engine's Foliage Painting Tool allowed hand-crafted placement where finer detail and artistic control were needed.

items.q: What visual effects and artistic modes does SplatGarden use?
alt: What effects are in the garden?
What do the click effects look like?
Are there Matisse and Seurat styles?
items.a: In Houdini, the team manipulated splat attributes and applied particle and pyro simulations with the GSOPs plugin. The interactive experience includes eight effects, such as dissolves, slime molds, vortex drift, chromatic ripples, and scan lines. Three full-screen painterly modes create Monet-style wet paint, Matisse-style posterized color with bold edges, and Seurat-style pointillist dots.

items.q: What technology powers SplatGarden in the browser?
alt: How does the web version work?
What tools power the live experience?
items.a: The browser experience uses the Spark splat renderer with Three.js, Vite 6 for builds, and OpenUSD for scene data. MediaPipe handles gesture recognition, while GPU shaders create interactive particle and click effects. An EffectComposer applies full-screen visual styling.

items.q: Who created SplatGarden?

items.a: The team includes Ben Jones, Itim Kongsakulvatanasook, Xinyi Liang, Yiyi Long, Danci Shen, Yichen Shi, and Yiqi Zheng. Their listed programs span visual effects, interactive design and game development, and animation. Dr. Deborah R. Fowler served as supervising professor.
